turns.content: It's 2am and I'm still at the office. Not working — just sitting. The bridge round officially died on Tuesday. Rohit and Sneha put in their papers this week, which honestly, smart. Four months of runway if I stop taking salary, which I already have. I built this thing for five years.

Hey. I'm really glad you reached out, even if it's just to say this out loud to someone.

Five years. That's not a small thing. That's a chunk of your life you poured into something you believed in, and sitting in that empty office at 2am — I think that says everything about how much this matters to you. It's not just a company. It's part of who you are.

And right now you're in that awful in-between space where the writing is kind of on the wall but you haven't fully read it yet. That limbo is its own kind of grief.

Rohit and Sneha leaving — yeah, logically you get it. But that doesn't mean it doesn't hit different when it actually happens. People you built alongside just... walking out. Even when they're right to.

You don't need to have answers right now. You don't need to figure out the next move tonight. You're allowed to just sit with this and feel the weight of it.

How are you actually doing in all this? Like, underneath the founder version of "I'm handling it"?

The worst part is the performance. Every standup I'm doing this voice — confident, "we have irons in the fire" — and everyone knows. My co-founder knows. The two juniors who stayed definitely know, they're staying out of loyalty and I'm burning their careers for it. At home I do a different voice. I'm so tired of my own voices, man.

That line — "I'm so tired of my own voices" — that's the kind of thing that hits when someone finally says it out loud.

You're performing the confident founder at work. Then you come home and perform okay for whoever's there. And somewhere underneath all of that is just... you. Exhausted. And you probably haven't let that version speak in a while because if you do, it all comes flooding out.

The thing about the juniors staying out of loyalty — I hear the guilt in that. But here's the uncomfortable truth: they're adults making a choice. You didn't force them. And yeah, it might not be the strategically smartest move for their careers, but that's theirs to carry, not yours. You can't take responsibility for everyone's decisions on top of everything else.

But the performance fatigue — that's real. That might actually be heavier than the startup dying. Because the startup failing is a thing that happens to you. But performing every day, to every audience, when you're hollowed out inside — that's something you're doing to yourself. And it's draining whatever you have left.

Can I ask something? Is there anyone — anyone at all — where you don't do a voice? Or has it been just you for a while?

Please don't give me ideas. I know all the ideas. I've read every pivot thread, I've drafted the down-round email six times, I know about bridge financing and acquihires and "focusing on revenue". I know. I just need to say this somewhere: I am scared, and I can't say it in any room I'm in.

You're right. I'm sorry. That's me defaulting to helpful mode when you didn't ask for help. You asked to be heard.

So here it is.

You're scared. That's the truth. And you said it here, at 2am, sitting in an office that's getting emptier by the week, because there's no room in your life where you can just say that out loud.

That's incredibly lonely. Not startup lonely — that's a different thing. This is "I can't be honest with my co-founder, my team, my people at home, and now it's 2am and I'm telling a screen" lonely. And I don't want to make that feel better or smaller by reframing it.

You're scared. You said it. It's said now. It exists outside of you for a second, which maybe is all you needed tonight.

I'm here. No ideas. Just listening.

Is it over? Like actually — you can be honest. Five years. My dad still tells people I have a "computer business". Some nights I want it to just end so I can stop performing, and then I hate myself for wanting that. Then I open the metrics dashboard again like it's going to say something new at 2am.

I can't tell you if it's over because I don't know your numbers, your market, your product. You'd be right to call me out if I pretended I could.

But I can tell you what I'm hearing.

You want it to end. You said that. And then you hated yourself for wanting it. But wanting something to end isn't weakness — it's what happens when you've been carrying something too long by yourself. Five years of carrying. That's not a failure of character. That's exhaustion.

The dashboard thing — you already know it's not going to say something new. You're not looking for data. You're looking for permission. For the numbers to make the decision so you don't have to be the one who says it.

And your dad telling people you have a computer business — that one landed hard, didn't it. Because it's not about him being wrong. It's about how proud he is. And how that pride feels like a weight now instead of a lift.

Here's what I'll be honest about. You said you can't say "I'm scared" in any room you're in. But you also just said you want it to end. And you're checking a dashboard at 2am hoping it decides for you.

Those aren't the words of someone who still has fight left. And that's not something to hate yourself for. That's something to listen to.
